name: Lena Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Lena, thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Per and I run a small dairy at Lindholm, forty-five cows and about a hundred ewes on the rough ground. Milking is at five and again at four in our old herringbone parlour, that's the kind where the cows stand in two angled rows and you work in the pit between them. In between I feed the calves, do the milk records and the books, and Per does the fieldwork. I love the calves and the routine, and what wears me down is milking twice a day every day of the year, Christmas included.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Thin. The milk price went down again in the spring and we're living month to month, maybe three weeks ahead at best. We own the house and half the land, the rest is rented from the church. Now and then I use one of those AI programs to check the milk buyer's contract or write a letter, my daughter set it up, but I'm careful with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: We'll go through five pictures of the future, one at a time. This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, it helps a bit with the paperwork. I'd say that at the choir and on the village show committee. I'm not online much, just the family group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it'd be fine. Our worries are the milk price and how long Per's knees will last in the pit. The computers were never going to fix either of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as we are. I'd keep using the program for letters, now and then. Nothing new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Things as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're careful with the AI program. Careful how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check what it says against the paper. It told me once that a cow gives milk for eighteen months after calving, and I thought, you've never met my Rosie. So I use it, but I don't trust it with anything that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the next few years look like for you and Per?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Milking twice a day till one of us can't. Then maybe sell the cows and keep the sheep. We'd decide that in a few years, not now.

S0.say: I'd say it's what I expected, because it helps a bit with paperwork. I'd say that at choir and on the village show committee.
S0.think: It'd be fine, because our real worries are the milk price and Per's knees. Computers were never going to fix either.
S0.do: Carries on milking and farming as usual and uses the AI program for letters now and then. Plans to decide in a few years whether to sell the cows and keep the sheep.
S0.feel: Calm, with things carrying on as normal.
S0.quote: It told me once that a cow gives milk for eighteen months after calving, and I thought, you've never met my Rosie.
S0.fieldNote: Lena uses AI cautiously and checks it against paper, with a nice story about her cow Rosie. Her worries are the milk price and her husband's knees. She's already quietly planning an eventual exit from dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more change. This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress and farms have always changed. The ones who adapt will be fine. But I'd also say families need to stick together, not leave each other behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it'd come to dairy first, with robot milkers. We'd have to decide whether to get one or stop milking. And that's a big decision at our age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go and look at robot milkers on farms nearby that already have them, and talk to the families running them. If they worked, I'd ask the milk buyer if they have a scheme to help pay. I wouldn't jump first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A big decision coming but not today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has anyone near you got a robot milker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The Brandts, two villages over, have had one for four years. Hanne Brandt told me she's slept past five every day since, and she cried the first morning. That sticks with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for one, with three weeks of money in hand?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan, if the milk buyer helped, or second-hand. I wouldn't put the house up for it. If it couldn't be done, we'd sell the cows.

S1.say: I'd say it's progress, farms have always changed, and those who adapt will be fine. But families need to stick together and not leave each other behind.
S1.think: It'd come to dairy first with robot milkers, and we'd have to choose between getting one or stopping milking. That's a big decision at our age.
S1.do: Visits nearby farms with robot milkers and talks to the families running them. If they work, asks the milk buyer about a scheme to help pay, but refuses to risk the house.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a big decision ahead but not yet.
S1.quote: Hanne Brandt told me she's slept past five every day since, and she cried the first morning.
S1.fieldNote: For Lena, a robot milker is a possible relief, not just a threat, and Hanne Brandt's story makes that real. She wants proof and help with costs before she moves. Her line on families sticking together reflects her traditional values.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This next one is very fast. This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and people need to look after their own. I'd say communities and churches need to help each other, not wait for the government. I wouldn't make a scene, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm scared. If big robot dairies can make milk cheaper, the buyer drops small farms like ours. Two years isn't enough to change anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every cost in the first year, no new things, no holiday. I'd talk to the milk buyer about how long our contract would last. And if it looked bad, I'd sell the cows while they still had a value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing sleep over the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the cows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, within the first year. I've milked those cows twice a day for thirty years, and I'd sell them in a morning to save the house. We'd keep the sheep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you lean on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first. Our daughter is a nurse, she'd help us with what she could. And the church, which owns half our land, I'd ask them to be patient on the rent.

S2.say: I'd say it's too fast and people need to look after their own, with communities and churches helping each other rather than waiting for government. I wouldn't make a scene.
S2.think: I'm scared, because if robot dairies make milk cheaper, the buyer drops small farms like ours. Two years isn't enough to change anything.
S2.do: Cuts every cost in the first year and asks the milk buyer how long their contract will last. Sells the cows within the year if it looks bad, keeping the sheep, and asks family and the church for help.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep over the milk contract.
S2.quote: I've milked those cows twice a day for thirty years, and I'd sell them in a morning to save the house.
S2.fieldNote: Lena would sell the herd quickly to protect the house, which shows how clear-eyed she is. Her support network is family and the church, which is also her landlord. She wants community, not state, to carry people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now with more time. This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to prepare, so let's not panic. I'd say families should plan together. I'd say it at the show committee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is enough to decide properly. We'd be sixty-three, and we might just get through if we're careful. I'm still worried about the milk price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at a second-hand robot milker once the neighbours have shown theirs work, and see if the milk buyer helps with the cost. I'd pay down the overdraft and try to put a little by. And I'd talk to the family about what happens to the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. A second-hand robot, three more years of milk, then sell the herd with the robot in the deal. That's the plan I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still sell the cows?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son is an apprentice electrician, maybe he could learn the robots. I'd ask him, but I wouldn't push.

S3.say: I'd say we have time to prepare, so let's not panic, and families should plan together. I'd say it at the show committee.
S3.think: Five years is enough to decide properly, and at sixty-three we might get through if we're careful. I still worry about the milk price.
S3.do: Looks at a second-hand robot milker once the neighbours' prove themselves and asks the milk buyer to help with cost. Pays down the overdraft, saves a little and talks to the family about the farm's future.
S3.quote: A second-hand robot, three more years of milk, then sell the herd with the robot in the deal.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Lena move from selling to investing, with a clever plan to sell the herd with the robot included. She'd wait for proof before buying. Her son's apprenticeship gives her a gentle hope she won't push.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, so prepare and work hard. I'd tell the young people to learn a trade that needs hands. And I'd say families should help each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For us it's mostly fine. We'd probably have stopped milking by then anyway. It's the young ones I'd worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep milking, look at a robot when it's proven and the price is right. I'd help our son with his electrician apprenticeship, maybe he'd add robot work to it. Around 2032 we'd start thinking about selling the herd.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A bit, for the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be sixty-eight in 2036. What does the farm look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheep and a few calves. I'd like to wake up one day of my life without a cow waiting for me. And maybe the robots would give us that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the young people at church?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn a trade, work hard, keep your faith. And stay close to your family. That never changes.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a long time, so prepare, work hard and help each other. I'd tell young people to learn a trade that needs hands.
S4.think: For us it's mostly fine, because we'd probably have stopped milking by then. It's the young ones I'd worry about.
S4.do: Keeps milking and looks at a robot milker once it's proven and affordable. Supports her son's electrician apprenticeship and plans to sell the herd around 2032.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, mostly for the young ones.
S4.quote: I'd like to wake up one day of my life without a cow waiting for me.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years puts AGI past Lena's milking years, and she even sees robots as a possible relief. Her advice to young people is about trade, faith and family. The wish to wake one day without a cow waiting is a quiet, honest admission of tiredness.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. The robots aren't the enemy, it's the buyer's letter saying they don't need our milk any more. What would help is a fair milk contract for small farms, and help to buy a robot second-hand.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About the animals. Who would notice a cow that's not right? A robot might, I suppose. But I'd still want a person to walk round.

headlineQuote: The robots aren't the enemy, it's the buyer's letter saying they don't need our milk any more.
portrait: Lena Olsen is a 58-year-old dairy farmer who milks forty-five cows twice a day with her husband Per and keeps sheep on rough ground. They live month to month, own their house and half their land, and rent the rest from the church. She uses AI for letters now and then but checks it against paper. She values family, faith and community over government help. She is calm about a plateau, uneasy about steady change, alarmed by fast AGI because the milk buyer could drop small farms, and with more time she plans a second-hand robot milker and an orderly sale of the herd.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the milk buyer could drop small farms before she has time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: A fair milk contract for small farms and help to buy a second-hand robot milker.
